description: Our name is a tribute to the historic Apollo 13 mission by NASA in 1970. While the astronauts famously said "Houston, we have a problem," our team flips the narrative. Facing the challenge of microgravity combustion, we are here to say: "Houston, we have a solution." Combining physics, engineering, and data analysis, we aim to accurately model the behavior of a spherical flame in free fall to contribute to the future of space safety and orbital research.
summary:
Flame in Freefall is an AI-powered fire safety platform that predicts material flammability, flame spread and toxic gas emissions in microgravity, built on NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) data.

In 0g there is no buoyancy, so flames become spherical, can smolder longer and produce hard-to-predict levels of carbon monoxide. Terrestrial fire models cannot be applied directly, and raw NASA experimental data takes deep expertise to interpret.

Users configure a spacecraft cabin with pure polymers (PMMA, PTFE, Nomex, cotton, PVC) or custom mixtures, set oxygen, ventilation and pressure, and get a forecast: Fire Risk Index, threat level, flame spread rate, peak temperature and CO over time. The model also flags the wick effect, when molten plastic is held by a charring fabric. An AI expert grounded in NASA reports (BASS-II, Saffire, ACME, SoFIE, FLEX-2) explains the results and suggests firefighting tactics, citing the source report and page.

This matters as Artemis plans a Moon Base at 30% oxygen or more, where materials burn far more easily than on Earth.
details:
Flame in Freefall is an interactive fire-safety simulation dashboard and Super Intelligence (SI) advisor for crewed spacecraft missions (ISS, Lunar Gateway, Orion). In microgravity (0g), the absence of buoyancy-driven convection means low-speed cabin ventilation (0.3–5.0 cm/s) feeds flames rather than cooling them, while molten polymers boil and eject burning droplets.

HOW IT WORKS AND KEY FEATURES

- Cabin and Mixture Simulator: adjusts O2 (15–30%), airflow (0–20 cm/s) and pressure (55–105 kPa) in real time to compute a 1.0–10.0 Fire Risk Index and threat status. Models single polymers (PMMA, Cotton, PVC, Nomex, PTFE) and normalized multi-component mixtures, accounting for Le Chatelier effective MOC in 0g, combined toxicity, and the 0g wick effect (synergy between melting polymers and fibrous or charring substrates).

- Source-Grounded Hybrid RAG: distilled summaries of NASA PSI reports (BASS-II, Saffire, ACME, SoFIE, FLEX-2) and historical incidents (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir) are indexed locally on CPU in ChromaDB via ParentDocumentRetriever with strict boolean material tags (has_pmma, has_cotton, etc.). Sensor telemetry is handled deterministically with Pandas and Plotly.

- Onboard SI Fire Advisor: combines live cabin telemetry with retrieved NASA PSI excerpts to provide tailored firefighting protocols (ventilation shutdown, inerting, fine water mist vs. CO2, breathing apparatus protection) with strict elemental guardrails. Every answer cites the source report and page.

TECH STACK

Python 3.11–3.12, Streamlit, LangChain, ChromaDB, HuggingFace (paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2), Pandas, Plotly, Google Gemini API.

WHY IT MATTERS

Artemis and future Mars missions will rely on habitats and rovers with oxygen-enriched, reduced-pressure atmospheres, where materials ignite and spread fire more easily. Fire has already threatened crews on Apollo 1, Apollo 13 and Mir. Our tool turns decades of microgravity combustion research into fast, cited answers for spacecraft designers and safety engineers.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Trust: every SI answer is grounded in and linked to NASA sources, while all physics and telemetry are calculated deterministically by our code. Scope: PSI has no partial-gravity combustion data yet, so we do not claim lunar-gravity predictions. Limits: the free Streamlit Cloud tier has 1 GB of RAM, so the physics forecast runs live online while the full RAG advisor is shown in our screenshots and demo.

SI DISCLOSURE

LLM tools were integrated as the onboard RAG advisor and used during development to assist with coding, documentation, and distilling NASA PSI technical reports into structured summaries.
